results.mechanistic_reasoning: The documented failure is valve mechanism failure causing incorrect tidal volume delivery. results.proposed_modification: Replace the multifilar coaxial lead design with a polymer-jacketed, single-filar, high-strength alloy conductor (e.g., MP35N) encased in a redundant insulation layer (e.g., silicone + ETFE).
results.mechanistic_reasoning: Lead fracture in ICDs is primarily driven by cyclic mechanical stress from cardiac motion over long dwell times (8+ years). The current multifilar coaxial design distributes stress across multiple thin wires, which can fatigue individually. A single-filar, high-strength alloy (e.g., MP35N) reduces internal friction and stress concentration points, while a polymer jacket (as used in CTO venoplasty guidewires, SOURCE 9) adds structural reinforcement. Redundant insulation (silicone + ETFE) mitigates insulation abrasion, a known contributor to lead failure. SOURCE 2 shows that older lead age (longer dwell time) correlates with extraction complexity, implying material degradation over time.
results.expected_effect: The modification will reduce the incidence of conductor fracture and insulation failure under cyclic cardiac motion, maintaining lead integrity for 8+ years. The polymer jacket and redundant insulation will resist mechanical and environmental stress, as demonstrated by the durability of polymer-jacketed guidewires in high-stress vascular interventions (SOURCE 9).
results.falsification_test: Implant the modified lead in a porcine model (as in SOURCE 6) and subject it to accelerated cyclic bending (e.g., 10^8 cycles at 1 Hz, mimicking 3+ years of cardiac motion). Compare fracture rates and electrical continuity to baseline multifilar coaxial leads under identical conditions.
results.why_different_from_baseline: The baseline uses multiple thin wires (multifilar) in a coaxial arrangement, which are prone to inter-filar friction and individual wire fatigue. The proposed design uses a single, high-strength conductor with a polymer jacket and redundant insulation, eliminating internal friction and adding structural resilience.

results.mechanistic_reasoning: The modification addresses the failure mechanism by enabling direct, minimally invasive removal of infectious material (e.g., biofilms, vegetations) from the pocket without full device explantation. results.why_different_from_baseline: The baseline (antibiotic-impregnated pouch) is passive and preventive, whereas this modification is active and therapeutic, enabling intervention *after* infection onset to avoid explantation.

results.proposed_modification: Replace the over-the-wire LV lead with a leadless LV pacing electrode deployed in the coronary sinus via a delivery catheter, eliminating the need for a permanent transvenous lead.
results.mechanistic_reasoning: The documented failure is LV lead fracture due to mechanical stress on the transvenous lead in the coronary sinus. Evidence shows that conductor externalization (a form of lead fracture) in LV coronary sinus leads causes irreversible electrical failure (SOURCE 2: "conductor externalization is a recognized mechanism of transvenous lead failure... extracted LV lead displayed conductor externalization"). Additionally, retained guidewires or mechanical complications from traditional lead placement can cause fractures or perforations (SOURCE 10: "Fracture and Perforation of Coronary Sinus Lead due to Retained Guide Wire"). A leadless electrode deployed in the coronary sinus would eliminate the long, flexible conductor prone to fatigue, externalization, or mechanical damage, as it would not rely on a continuous transvenous lead body. Cross-domain evidence from subcutaneous/extravascular ICDs demonstrates that eliminating transvenous leads reduces lead-related complications (SOURCE 6: "efforts are being made to introduce defibrillation and pacing interventions through a single device called the modular cardiac rhythm management system (mCRM)").
results.expected_effect: The modification would reduce the incidence of LV lead fractures by removing the primary failure mechanism (mechanical stress on a transvenous conductor). This would maintain lead integrity and CRT therapy delivery over 8+ years, as the leadless electrode would not be subject to the same fatigue or externalization risks.
results.falsification_test: Implant a leadless LV pacing electrode in the coronary sinus of a porcine model and subject it to cyclic mechanical stress (e.g., 10^8 cycles of bending/torsion simulating 8+ years of cardiac motion). Compare the incidence of electrical failure (impedance >3000 Ω or loss of capture) to a traditional over-the-wire LV lead under identical conditions. If the leadless electrode fails at a rate statistically indistinguishable from the traditional lead, the hypothesis is falsified.
results.why_different_from_baseline: The baseline is an over-the-wire LV lead, which requires a continuous transvenous conductor prone to fatigue and externalization. The proposed modification uses a leadless electrode, which has no permanent transvenous conductor, thus eliminating the primary failure mode.
